clue.text: Cloud of choking smoke leads to black vegetable

parts.note: pother is an old word for a choking cloud of smoke or dust
B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils

explanation.surface: Smog from a fire ends up blackening the garden greens.
explanation.definitionFit: A pot-herb is any leafy plant grown for the cooking pot, a kitchen green.

clue.text: Poignancy of quiet mounted guardsman?

parts.note: P is piano, the musical direction for quiet
Athos is one of Dumas's Three Musketeers, the king's mounted guards

explanation.surface: A mounted soldier on silent sentry duty is a touching sight.
explanation.definitionFit: Pathos is the quality that arouses pity or sorrow, i.e. emotional poignancy.

clue.text: Stone mullion in correct position to cut, reportedly

indicators.note: reportedly means the words are said aloud and what is heard spells the answer

parts.note: true means in correct position and mow means cut, giving true-mow when spoken

explanation.surface: A mason checks a stone upright is set straight before trimming it.
explanation.walkthrough: TRUE (in correct position) plus MOW (cut) is said aloud as the French word TRUMEAU.
explanation.definitionFit: A trumeau is the central stone pillar dividing a doorway or window, much like a mullion.

clue.text: A wizard giving directions on the Scottish pipe

parts.note: E is east, a compass direction
N is north, another compass direction
the chanter is the fingered melody pipe of the Scottish bagpipes

explanation.surface: A magician gives orders to a bagpiper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'directions' supplies two compass points, E and N, before the chanter, the melody pipe of a bagpipe.
explanation.definitionFit: An enchanter is one who casts spells, a sorcerer.

clue.text: Birdfood to come out of earnings — blimey!

parts.note: bread is slang for money or earnings
crumbs and blimey are both mild British exclamations of surprise

explanation.surface: Someone is startled at having to fund bird food out of their wages.
explanation.definitionFit: Crumbled bread scattered outdoors is a classic feed for garden birds.

clue.text: One gin could catch a poacher

definitions.text: One gin could catch a poacher

parts.note: one, as in 'one should', means a man or person
a gin is a snare or trap for game

explanation.surface: A single snare set by a gamekeeper might be enough to nab an intruder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gin' suggests the drink, but here it is the old word for a snare; the whole clue also describes the steel trap once set for poachers.
explanation.definitionFit: A man-trap was a sprung steel jaw laid on estates to seize trespassers and thieves of game.

clue.text: November the fifth and no old penny for the guy!

indicators.note: the fifth means the letter in fifth place of the month's name is taken
no means the coin's letter is removed from the little word beside it

parts.note: D was the symbol for a penny in British pre-decimal money

explanation.surface: Bonfire Night, the fifth of November, has children begging a penny for the guy.
explanation.walkthrough: Guy Fawkes Night is 5 November, when children once asked 'a penny for the guy'. Here 'the fifth' takes M, the fifth letter of November; AND without D gives AN.
explanation.definitionFit: Guy is informal for a fellow or chap.

clue.text: Name on house erected in S. France

indicators.note: erected, in a down clue, means the word is built upwards, so it reads bottom to top

parts.note: a semi is a semi-detached house

explanation.surface: A nameplate goes up on a house in the south of France.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down answer 'erected' turns SEMI upside down to give IMES. A semi is a British semi-detached house.
explanation.definitionFit: Nimes is a Roman city in the Gard department of southern France.

clue.text: Rope in a greenhorn

definitions.meaning: to rope in is to enlist or draw someone into joining
a greenhorn is a raw novice, a new enlistee

explanation.definitionFit: To enlist someone is to sign them up, and a raw new enlistee is called the same word.

clue.text: Do they settle for tea?

parts.note: colonial settlers who set up estates to grow the tea crop, read as people who 'settle for' it

explanation.surface: Asking who will accept a cup of tea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'settle for' suggests accepting something second-best; read literally, it is colonists settling land to grow tea.
explanation.definitionFit: Planters were colonists who settled land and ran estates growing tea, sugar or rubber.

clue.text: Right about getting meal without a starter in police club!

indicators.note: about means the abbreviation for right is turned round to face the other way
without a starter means the first letter of the word for the meal is dropped

parts.note: luncheon is a formal word for a midday meal

explanation.surface: Someone corrects a lunch order that lacks a first course, at a police social club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without a starter' looks like menu talk but removes the L of LUNCHEON, leaving UNCHEON; 'about' turns RT into TR.
explanation.definitionFit: A truncheon is the short baton or cosh carried by police officers.

clue.text: Coffee put second to tea?

parts.note: mo is short for moment, a second
cha (char) is British slang for tea

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether coffee ranks behind tea.
explanation.definitionFit: Mocha is a kind of coffee, originally shipped from the Yemeni port of that name.

clue.text: A herring, we hear, is a shorter version of one

definitions.text: A herring, we hear, is a shorter version of one

parts.words: A herring, we hear, is a shorter version of one
parts.note: with the h dropped, Cockney style, 'a herring' is heard as 'a 'erring', i.e. a ring, and The Ring is the short title of Wagner's huge stage work

explanation.surface: A fish name, spoken aloud, turns out to be an abbreviation.
explanation.walkthrough: Say 'a herring' without its h: 'a ring'. The Ring is the shortened title of Wagner's Der Ring des Nibelungen, a work of the kind the answer names.
explanation.definitionFit: Wagner's Ring cycle is a set of four musical dramas sung on stage throughout.

clue.text: Formal wear put on going to clubs, say?

parts.note: to dress is to put clothes on
clubs is an example of a suit in a pack of cards

explanation.surface: Someone smartens up before an evening out at the nightclubs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clubs' suggests nightclubs; it is one of the four card suits.
explanation.definitionFit: A dress suit is a man's evening tailcoat outfit, worn for white-tie occasions.

clue.text: Mingle penal reform with enrolling juries

indicators.note: reform means the letters of the two words are formed again in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Penal reform mixed with the process of swearing in jurors.
explanation.definitionFit: Empanelling is listing people on a panel, especially selecting a jury.

clue.text: As an alternative to laser, trust damp poultice!

indicators.note: an alternative arrangement means the letters of these three words are put in another order

explanation.surface: Rather than laser treatment, a patient is advised to rely on a moist compress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'alternative' is the signal that LASER, TRUST and DAMP are rearranged; 'As an' and 'to' are joining words.
explanation.definitionFit: A mustard plaster was an old home remedy, a paste of mustard spread on cloth and laid on the chest.

clue.text: A worker I rely on, being opposed to monopolies

parts.note: a worker is a worker ant, a crossword staple
to rely on someone is to trust them

explanation.surface: An employee is someone the speaker depends on to fight big business.
explanation.definitionFit: Antitrust laws, in American usage, prohibit monopolies and cartels.

clue.text: Loss-assessor is reasonable in replacement of dear pieces

indicators.note: in means the word for fair is put inside the scrambled letters
replacement of means the letters of the word are rearranged into new places

parts.note: just means fair or reasonable

explanation.surface: An insurance man fairly costs the replacement of valuable items.
explanation.walkthrough: 'replacement of' signals the anagram of the second word; 'pieces' only rounds off the surface, and 'Loss-assessor' is an insurance term.
explanation.definitionFit: An insurance adjuster assesses the size of a claim after a loss.

clue.text: In sight, hearing and taste

parts.note: the faculty of telling things apart operates in every sense, and in the arts it is also refined judgement

explanation.surface: A list of the senses.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as the senses, but it describes the power to distinguish fine differences, which also means good taste.
explanation.definitionFit: Discernment, the ability to tell fine differences apart, works through the senses and also means refined judgement.

clue.text: Sort of jab sustained in Barking party?

definitions.text: Sort of jab sustained in Barking party?

parts.words: Sort of jab sustained in Barking party?
parts.note: a dig, or jab, to the leg bone that you might suffer when barking it, scraping the skin, at a rowdy do

explanation.surface: Someone is jabbed at a party in Barking, a district of east London.
explanation.walkthrough: Barking is an east London district, but 'barking' a shin means scraping it; a dig to the shin is a lively party.
explanation.definitionFit: A shindig is a noisy, lively party or celebration.

clue.text: Part of act by old boy is blue

parts.note: OB is the abbreviation for old boy, a former pupil
an act of a play is divided into scenes

explanation.surface: An elderly man's turn in a play is risque.
explanation.definitionFit: Blue jokes or films are indecent ones.

clue.text: Caught by almost any person in the gully

parts.note: C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

indicators.note: almost means the word stops one letter short of its end

parts.note: anyone means any person

explanation.surface: Anyone at all might be caught fielding in the gully, a close cricket position.
explanation.walkthrough: Gully is a cricket fielding position, which the surface plays on; 'almost' drops the final E of ANYONE.
explanation.definitionFit: A canyon is a deep, steep-sided ravine, a large gully.

clue.text: Catholic values in royal training

indicators.note: training puts these letters through a drill until they take a new shape

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for royal, as in RN or RAF

explanation.surface: A Catholic upbringing is part of a prince's education.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Catholic' looks like the religion; with a small c it means all-embracing, which is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Catholic with a small c means all-embracing or wide-ranging, a synonym.

clue.text: Brilliant success in city almost overdue

parts.note: EC is the postcode area of the City of London

indicators.note: almost means the last letter of the word is cut off

parts.note: late means overdue

explanation.surface: A big achievement in town arrives only just behind schedule.
explanation.definitionFit: Eclat is a dazzling triumph or display of brilliance.

clue.text: Soprano out of place in Rigoletto's cast

indicators.note: in means the letters sit inside the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: A singer from another work is wrongly listed among Verdi's Rigoletto cast.
explanation.walkthrough: The role is from Puccini, not Verdi, so she is 'out of place' in that cast, a phrase that only joins.
explanation.definitionFit: Puccini's heroine of that name is a leading role sung by a soprano.

clue.text: Coming and going in waves?

parts.note: the ebb and flow of the sea, rising and falling twice a day

explanation.surface: Something that arrives and leaves in surges.
explanation.definitionFit: The sea's twice-daily ebb and flow comes in and goes out, waves and all.

clue.text: Comfortable in Hawaiian garland, of course

parts.note: a lei is a Hawaiian flower necklace
of course means certainly or surely

explanation.surface: A holidaymaker is naturally at ease wearing island flowers.
explanation.definitionFit: A comfortable, unhurried pace is a relaxed and easy one.

clue.text: Notedly, a meadow of lindens?

parts.note: a grassy field of lime trees, famous in music from Vaughan Williams's song Linden ...

explanation.surface: A musical question about a field of lime trees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Notedly' points to music: Vaughan Williams's song 'Linden Lea'. The word is a poetic term for a meadow.
explanation.definitionFit: Lea is a poetic word for a field of grass or pasture.

clue.text: Moving target, a sporting event between banks

indicators.note: moving shifts the letters of the words around into a new order

explanation.surface: A shooting contest with a moving target is held on a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moving target' is a familiar phrase, but 'Moving' rearranges TARGET and A; 'between banks' means on a river.
explanation.definitionFit: A regatta is a series of boat races, held on a river between its two shores.

clue.text: Old guitar, fitted with new head, would have been a boomer

indicators.note: giving the bird a different first letter yields the instrument, as the clue's change of head describes

parts.note: the bittern is a marsh bird famous for its booming call

explanation.surface: An old instrument, rebuilt with a new top, would once have boomed.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue runs backwards: give the old guitar's name the head B in place of G and you get the booming bird. 'boomer' sounds like a loud instrument but is the bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The gittern was a small medieval stringed instrument, an ancestor of the modern guitar.
